Web3 Does Not Have One Customer. That Is Why Most Launch Plans Break.

By lowob · 25 August 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Strategy / Web3

A Web3 product can attract thousands of people to a launch announcement and still have almost nobody using it a month later. One reason is straightforward: the project reached an audience, but not necessarily the people needed to make the product useful.

Unlike a simple consumer app, a protocol may need several groups to participate before it works as intended. Users, developers, liquidity providers, ecosystem partners and institutions may each be waiting for evidence from someone else. A launch plan should solve those dependencies, not simply announce to everyone at once.

Start with the people who make the product work

The original article mapped six groups: users, developers and integrators, capital and liquidity providers, distribution partners, institutional stakeholders, and community or governance participants. Not every project needs all six. A wallet app and a regulated asset platform have very different needs.

Write down the role each group plays. Users need a clear reason to try the product. Developers need documentation and a reliable way to integrate. Capital providers need to understand risk and economic incentives. A distribution partner needs to know what it gains by introducing the product to customers. Institutions need credible operating and compliance information.

That is more useful than treating everyone as a single group called “the community.” The same announcement is unlikely to answer all of those questions.

Launch in the order your product actually needs

Consider a hypothetical tokenized asset platform. A broad marketing campaign might create awareness, but it would not replace custody arrangements, onboarding requirements, or a way for investors to access the product.

A sensible sequence might be: confirm the legal and custody model; secure an anchor distribution or liquidity partner; test onboarding with a limited group; document the issues; and only then expand public promotion. The exact order depends on the business. The principle is to identify what must be true before the next audience can act.

First: readiness

What needs to work for the first users or partners to participate?

Next: proof

Which successful integration, product action or operating result would make another group comfortable?

Then: distribution

Who can bring more of the right participants once that proof exists?

This is consistent with the distinction in a16z crypto's Web3 GTM framework: projects may need developers, partners and other stakeholders alongside end users, and token incentives alone do not guarantee lasting participation.

Keep one product truth, but change the explanation

Suppose the product makes it easier to access a particular financial instrument. A user wants to know what they can do and what it costs. A wallet integration team wants implementation details. A partner wants to understand demand and support obligations. An institution wants documentation, risk controls and accountability.

The product shouldn't tell four contradictory stories. It should explain one real capability in four useful ways. For each audience, write down the claim, evidence, next action and main reason they might hesitate. If the evidence doesn't exist yet, say that internally rather than filling the gap with marketing language.

Use a 90-day plan as a sequence, not a countdown

Days 1 to 30: Interview the participants who matter most. Identify blockers, test approved claims, make the first integration or onboarding process reliable and decide what success will look like.

Days 31 to 60: Work with a small group of real users and partners. Run developer sessions or product walkthroughs where relevant. Note where people get stuck and turn those objections into documentation and product fixes.

Days 61 to 90: Expand the channels and audience groups that have shown genuine activity. Announce partnerships when they create access or utility. Use creators and community programming to explain things people already need help understanding.

This is an illustrative sequence, not a promise that any Web3 project can reach launch readiness in exactly 90 days.

Measure useful participation, not just attention

Different participants need different measures. For users, that may be a first meaningful action and whether they return. For developers, successful integrations. For capital providers, committed versus actively used capital and its persistence. For partners, qualified introductions and downstream product use.

Link those outcomes to the cost of acquiring them where possible. A launch is not coordinated simply because every social account posted on the same day. It is coordinated when one group's participation makes the next group's participation more likely.

lowob takeaways

  • Map the actual participants. Don't treat users, builders, capital and partners as one audience.
  • Find the dependency chain. Make the thing the next group needs to trust or use before inviting them.
  • Tailor the proof. The product truth stays consistent, but each group needs different evidence.
  • Measure continuing use. A successful announcement is not the same as a working market.

Sources and notes

a16z crypto, Go-to-Market in Web3: New Mindsets, Tactics, Metrics. Background on stakeholder groups, community, incentives and GTM measurement.
